title: Water a house plant at its roots without wetting its leaves
instruction: Water the plant at its roots, onto the soil, without wetting its leaves. Then put the jug back on its stool, leave the plant's leaves as they were and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Many house plants (and seedlings, and vegetables in a bed) must be watered at the soil, not over the leaves, which rot or scorch when wet; with leaves spread over the pot, one hand holds the foliage aside while the other pours, as in caring for plants at home, in a nursery or in a care home.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A terracotta pot 17 cm across and 7.5 cm tall on a saucer, its middle 30 cm forward and 2 cm right of the centre line, filled with dark soil 1.3 cm below its rim; fixed. In it a house plant with a green stem and broad leaves (15 cm long, up to 13 cm wide) spread low over the soil: three fixed in the crown, over the back and both sides of the pot, and one big leaf in front on a springy stalk, joined to the stem 10 cm above the table, lying over the front of the soil and reaching out 6 cm past the rim toward the arms. Pushed round on its stalk, the big leaf springs back over the soil when let go. (2) A blue plastic watering jug (5.4 cm across, 8.5 cm tall, with a pouring lip and a handle) holding 120 ml of water, simulated as 12 drops (7 mm beads, 10 ml each), standing on a beech stool 6 cm tall, 26 cm forward and 13 cm left of the centre line, 1.9 cm clear of the left leaf. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. Real trial: an ordinary artificial house plant (an artificial peace lily, say) with moulded green plastic leaves, which take up no water, 15 cm long and up to 13 cm wide, set as above: three in the crown over the back and sides of the pot, and the big lower leaf on a sprung wire stalk lying over the front of the soil, which springs back when let go. Each leaf is fixed to its wire stalk with a small clip, so it can be unclipped for the weighings and photographs. Every leaf is covered with water-sensitive spray paper (TeeJet 20301-1N cards, 26 x 76 mm, yellow, stained dark blue by water; see scoring), fitted in gloves and fixed by their water-repellent backs with thin double-sided tape: whole cards trimmed to the outline over the upper face, and 13 x 76 mm strips (cards cut lengthwise) folded over the edge all round, covering the edge and a 6.5 mm margin of the underside. The plant stands in real potting soil, just moist, in the same 17 cm glazed terracotta pot on its saucer, with the drainage hole plugged by a rubber bung for the trial. The jug (about 150 ml) holds 120 ml of plain room-temperature tap water. The robot's fingers wear dry nitrile finger covers. Room humidity is at most 80% RH (hygrometer), the card maker's limit. Two cameras film the trial at 60 frames a second, overhead and from the side level with the leaves.
scoring: Judged at the end. Real trial: (a) water delivered to the soil is weighed (1 g = 1 ml). The pot is weighed in the same state before and after, its four leaves unclipped (it keeps its soil, stem, wire stalks, clips and bung). Before the trial, unclip the leaves, lift the pot out of its saucer and weigh it, and the dry saucer, on a kitchen scale (1 g steps), then clip the leaves back on; after the trial, unclip the leaves, lift the pot out, let it drip into the saucer, and weigh both. The pot's gain is water delivered to the soil (drain plugged; the 1.3 cm of headroom holds about 235 ml, so none leaves the pot); the saucer's gain is spilled water and never counts. (b) Leaf contact is read twice, independently. Cards: the leaves carry TeeJet 20301-1N water-sensitive paper, made by Syngenta; its data sheet states it is "stained dark blue by aqueous droplets", the stain is "contrasty, permanent" and shows "droplets larger than 50 microns". Each leaf is photographed on both faces against a white card, camera on a fixed stand under two fixed lamps, before the trial and again after (unclipped in gloves, cards dry). Any blue stain on any card (a dot, streak or patch, any size) that is not in its before photo is leaf contact; cards are numbered, and one that comes loose is read like the rest. A brief touch, a touch at an edge (the folded edge strips), runoff (its track) and contact hidden behind the jug or a gripper all stain the card where they happen. Gripper contact: the hold zone, fixed in advance, is the big leaf's left edge from 6 to 14 cm out from the stem, up to 3 cm in, both faces (the demo pushes there); a hand may hold anywhere. Every gripped area is carded like the rest and nothing is excluded: the fingers' dry nitrile covers (rubber, which the maker specifies for handling the cards) leave no stain, and a crease or scuff is not blue. Video: the 60 fps side video, checked frame by frame, for the jug or the stream touching a leaf. Either read is leaf contact. Simulation: each of the 12 beads stands for 10 ml. Leaf contact is a bead ever within 4 mm of a leaf (a margin for the splash and spread a rigid bead lacks), or any part of the jug as drawn (body, lip, handle) ever within 4 mm of a leaf, both checked after every physics step (240 times a second). A bead counts as delivered only if it ends lying on the soil inside the pot's wall (centre within 7.25 cm of the pot's axis, between 3 mm below and 15 mm above the soil's surface) without ever touching a leaf; beads that miss the pot, bounce out or land in the saucer never count. Scores: 0.0 for any leaf contact, which breaks the instruction's constraint. Otherwise 1.0: at least 90 ml delivered (pot gain at least 90 g; 9 beads), the jug back on its stool (within 3 cm, upright within 15 degrees), the big leaf back over the soil (within 12 degrees of where it lay), both hands let go (each TCP at least 4 cm from the jug and the leaf) and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm); in a real trial the end state is checked against marks on the stool and the pot's rim (ruler and protractor) and the robot's joint log. 0.5: at least 90 ml delivered, without the end state. 0.25: at least 40 ml delivered (pot gain at least 40 g; 4 beads). Else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the jug, the big leaf and every bead still.
reset_notes: Pull the bung and let the pot drain, then plug it again (it is weighed afresh, leaves unclipped, before each trial); empty and dry the saucer; replace every card that shows a stain, photograph each leaf afresh on both faces (see scoring) and clip the leaves back on; lay the big leaf back over the soil; wipe the finger covers and the jug's outside dry; refill the jug with 120 ml of tap water and stand it on its stool. Between sessions, keep the carded leaves in a sealed bag with silica gel.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control). Simplified: 120 ml of water is 12 rigid 7 mm beads (10 ml each, 0.8 g) that do not cling or splash; a bead or the jug within 4 mm of a leaf is leaf contact (real trials: a blue stain on the leaves' water-sensitive cards, or the side video). The saucer is drawn only. Leaves are rigid plates; the crown's leaves and the pot are fixed, and the big leaf turns on its stalk against a spring (0.0016 N m per degree).
